sentences.text: This dinosaur reached a length of about 18 meters and likely had a body structure similar to that of Saltasaurus.
Scientists estimate that the animal weighed approximately 30 tonnes.
Its leg bones were notably slender and graceful, differing from those seen in Titanosaurus and Antarctosaurus.
The femur and tibia were fifty percent larger than the corresponding bones found in Saltasaurus.
Some researchers have suggested that bony plates covered its back, though this connection remains uncertain.
If these plates existed, their ridges were much smaller than those observed on Saltasaurus.
Huene originally described the animal as a large yet elegantly built sauropod.
An egg of the genus Megaloolithus found in the Anacleto Formation might have been laid by Laplatasaurus instead of Titanosaurus.
The species was named after La Plata, Argentina, after its sole known specimen was discovered in the Anacleto Formation.
Friedrich von Huene introduced the name in 1927, but it was initially considered invalid because no formal description existed.
A proper description of the type species Laplatasaurus araukanicus finally appeared in 1929.
Huene constructed the genus based on broken fossils recovered from three separate sites within the Campanian-age Anacleto Formation.
In 1979, José Fernando Bonaparte chose a tibia and fibula, catalog number MLP 26-306, to serve as the lectotype, although they might belong to different individuals.
The collection contains two presacral vertebrae, twenty tail vertebrae with ten still connected, limb parts, shoulder girdle elements, and some juvenile remains.
Many other specimens were unearthed at the original site and at Rancho de Ávila in Los Alamitos, Río Negro.
These fossils are important because they mark the first reported evidence of armor on a sauropod.
Huene placed Laplatasaurus within the family Titanosauridae, a grouping that is still widely accepted today.
A study from 2015 indicated that the dinosaur was closely related to Bonitasaura, Futalognkosaurus, Mendozasaurus, and Uberabatitan.
This creature lived during the Late Cretaceous, roughly 75 million years ago, in the Campanian stage of what is now South America.
Its time range spans from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago during the Campanian stage.
It is currently debated whether all material assigned to L. araukanicus belongs to the same genus and species or to unknown forms, due to incomplete associated material.
